Your business plan, section by section

Ten parts make up your plan. Open any card to see what the section should say, what a strong answer looks like, and where to find evidence. Cards marked Needs research must be backed by evidence you source yourself, so start with the Research Hub.

New: Missions

Practice finding real numbers, building a target market story, and defending it the way a judge will ask. Study a winning pitch, then try the levels.

Also new: two games. Guess who buys from a real local business, then race a classmate to find numbers.

How to use this site

  • Write your plan in Google Docs or Slides. This site is a reference, not a place to save your work.
  • Tag every claim as data-backed (a real, cited source) or hypothesis (an informed guess you still need to test).
  • The examples use a made-up business so you can see the standard. Do not copy them. Replace every number with your own research.

Not sure what to look up?

Use the Research Helper: describe your idea or build a question from menus, and see where to find the evidence.

Research tools

Open a tool to start. Each card lists the plan sections it feeds.

Data-backed vs. hypothesis

  • Every claim in your pitch should end up tagged one of two ways.
  • Data-backed means it comes from a real, cited source: the Demographics tab, or one of the sources on the Psychographics and Business Landscape tabs.
  • Hypothesis means it's an informed guess, built from the closest available data, waiting to be tested with real customers later in the year.
  • Keeping that distinction visible (a simple two-column table works) is good practice for any pitch, and it's honest about what you actually know versus what you're betting on.
American Community Survey · 5-Year Estimates, 2020–2024

Demographics

Real Census data for Geographics and Demographics, plus the household-economics side of Business Landscape: population, income, education, housing, mobility, and more for San Francisco neighborhoods, Bay Area counties, California, and the nation.

Where this data comes from, and what "5-year estimate" means

This isn't a full count like the once-a-decade Census. It's the American Community Survey (ACS), a continuous household survey the Census Bureau mails, calls, and knocks on doors for, all year, every year. About 3.5 million addresses are randomly selected nationwide each year, with roughly 1.9 million completed interviews, on the order of 1 in 65 households in a given year. Scaled to San Francisco's ~364,000 households, that works out to somewhere around 5,000–6,000 SF households a year, or roughly 25,000–30,000 over five years (our own estimate, scaled from the Bureau's national rate, not a published city-level figure).

"5-year estimate" means every number here is blended from interviews collected across all of 2020–2024, not a single-year snapshot. The Census Bureau does this because small areas (like a single SF neighborhood) don't get enough interviews in any one year to produce a reliable number on their own. Pooling five years of interviews together builds up a big enough sample, at the cost of the number reflecting a 5-year period rather than "right now." This tool uses 5-year estimates for every tier, including the nation and the state, so every geography is measured the same way and can be fairly compared.

Because it's a sample and not a full count, every estimate carries a margin of error: smaller areas (like an SF neighborhood) have wider margins than larger ones (like the nation). See the "margin of error" section below for what that means for the numbers you're looking at right now.

Compare to a school

Every SFUSD high school is shown against the SFUSD district average. This is enrolled-student data from the California Department of Education, not the Census, so treat it as a companion view, not an apples-to-apples match with the neighborhood numbers above.

School SFUSD (district total)
Why these categories won't match the Census numbers above

This describes enrolled K-12 students at that school, not everyone living in the surrounding neighborhood, so it will not (and should not) match the Census numbers above. Race, ethnicity, and gender line up closely with the Census's own categories. The other three are proxies, not the same measurement: English Learner status counts a student currently learning English, not "born outside the US" (not the same as the Census "foreign-born" figure). Students with Disabilities is a special-education/IEP designation, not the Census's adult functional-disability question. Socioeconomically Disadvantaged counts a student who qualifies for free/reduced meals, has a parent without a high school diploma, or is in foster care: a broader, usually higher-reading measure than the Census poverty rate above.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey (ACS), 2020–2024 5-year estimates, pulled via the Census API. Dollar figures are inflation-adjusted to 2024.

School comparison: California Department of Education (CDE), 2025–26 Census Day enrollment data, pulled from DataQuest.

San Francisco neighborhoods are Census PUMAs (Public Use Microdata Areas), the smallest geography the ACS publishes detailed estimates for, each covering roughly 100,000–150,000 residents, so they group several real neighborhoods together rather than matching them one-to-one.

Psychographics · What do customers like outside of work?

Understanding how people spend their time and attention

No dataset answers "what does my customer like" directly. This is the category best confirmed later with real customer conversations. Until then, build an evidence-based persona from the sources below, and label every claim built from them as a hypothesis, not a fact.

Turning these into a persona claim

Every claim built from the sources below should read like a hypothesis, not a fact: "We believe our customers spend significant leisure time on Instagram, based on Pew's age-based usage data," not "our customers are on Instagram." Keep a simple two-column table in the business plan (Data-backed vs. Hypothesis) so it's clear which claims are measured and which are informed guesses waiting to be tested.

Business Landscape · How much do they spend, and who else is selling to them?

Category spending and the competitive landscape

The Demographics tab covers income and rent: spending capacity. This tab puts dollar figures on how households divide that spending across categories (BLS survey averages) and shows who is already selling to them (business counts). It does not tell you where your specific customer shops or what they would pay for your idea. That takes your own research (see the box below).

What this hub can’t tell you (and how to find out)

Public data describes averages for groups of households. It can’t see inside your customer’s head or wallet. Four questions every business plan needs sit mostly outside the data, so plan to collect them yourself:

  • Where does your customer shop? No free dataset covers this for a specific group. Use the competitor counts below to see who exists, then observe and ask: visit the places, count customers, and survey people in your segment.
  • What else might they buy? The spending table below shows which categories take big shares of a budget. Which products go together for your customer is a question for interviews and surveys.
  • What would they pay for a service? The data shows what households spend in a category, not what they would pay for yours. Test it: ask a price question in a survey, or try a pre-sale or a pop-up and see who actually pays.
  • How much do they spend on leisure per week? The table below gives a survey average (Entertainment, Food away from home). Treat it as a starting guess, then check it against what the people you survey say they spend.

Household spending by category

From the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey. Pick a national group that looks like your customer, and see how its spending compares with the San Francisco area average. Amounts are dollars per household (BLS calls it a “consumer unit”).

How to read this, and what to be careful about

The ratio idea. BLS publishes spending by age and income only for the whole U.S., and for San Francisco only for all households together. The SF ÷ U.S. ratio column shows how much higher (or lower) the SF area spends than the U.S. average in each category. If you tick “Apply the SF ratio,” the table multiplies the national figure for your chosen group by that ratio. That is an assumption (that your group differs from the national version of itself by the same factor as all SF households do), not a measurement. Say so in your plan.

“San Francisco” here is the 5-county metro area (San Francisco, Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, San Mateo), not the city. It is a 2023–24 two-year average from a small sample, so numbers can wobble.

Years differ. The national age and income columns are calendar year 2024. The SF and U.S.-all columns are the 2023–24 average, so the ratio compares like with like (both 2023–24).

Averages hide spread. An average household includes people who spend nothing in a category. Someone who actually buys the product spends more than the per-household figure.

No SF number? BLS publishes only some categories for metro areas. Where the SF column is blank, you can still use the national figure, but you cannot apply a ratio.

Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Expenditure Surveys (calendar-year 2024 tables by age and income; 2023–24 geographic tables for the San Francisco–Oakland–Hayward metro area and the U.S.).
